Lecture 18: The Exponential Function ​

Topics: §5.8 — Compound Interest Definition of e, Binomial Expansion to Power Series, Differential Equation y′=ky, Euler's Formula, Exponential of the Derivative as Shift, Matrix Exponential, Spectral Formula for eAs, Complex Eigenvalues as Rotation Date: May 14 – May 18, 2026

Overview ​

Lecture 17 introduced complex numbers so that the eigenvalue pipeline can continue over C:

det(tI−A)⟶factor into linear factors⟶spectral projections.

Lecture 18 introduces the exponential function from one principle:

eX=limn→∞(I+Xn)n.

The input X may be a real number, a complex number, a matrix, or even the derivative operator.

Input XExponential eXMeaning
real number xexgrowth or decay
complex number iθeiθ=cos⁡θ+isin⁡θrotation
matrix AeAssolves y′=Ay
derivative ddxesddxshifts functions by s

The repeated theme is:

TIP

Repeated tiny multiplicative nudges compound into a smooth transformation.

1. What Is e? ​

1.1 A Money Question ​

Start with $1 in a bank.

The bank offers 100% interest per year, computed linearly.

If the money stays untouched:

TimeBalance
after 1 year$2
after 2 years$3
after 1/2 year$1.50

But there is a trick.

Withdraw after one year and immediately redeposit. Then the second year's interest is computed on $2, not on $1:

after 2 years=2+1⋅2=4.

This beats the linear value 3.

Now withdraw halfway through the year and redeposit:

after half year=1+12=1.5,

then after the second half:

1.5+12(1.5)=2.25.

This beats 2.

1.2 Compound More Often ​

If we compound n times per year, each period has interest rate 1/n.

Each period multiplies the balance by

1+1n.

After n periods:

(1+1n)n.

The values are:

n(1+1n)n
12.000
22.250
42.441
102.594
1002.705
10002.717

The amount grows, but it does not become infinite. It approaches a number.

Proposition

The number e is defined by

e=limn→∞(1+1n)n=2.71828….

More generally, if the yearly rate is x, then each of n periods has rate x/n, so

ex=limn→∞(1+xn)n.

Attention

This is the definition of the exponential function in this lecture. The series, differential equation, Euler formula, matrix exponential, and Taylor theorem all come from this definition.

2. From Limit to Power Series ​

The limit definition explains what ex is, but it is not convenient for computation.

To compute, expand

(1+xn)n

by the binomial theorem:

(1+xn)n=1+n1!xn+n(n−1)2!x2n2+n(n−1)(n−2)3!x3n3+⋯.

Now inspect the coefficients.

The x coefficient is

nn=1.

The x2 coefficient has the factor

n(n−1)n2=nn⋅n−1n⟶1.

The x3 coefficient has the factor

n(n−1)(n−2)n3=nn⋅n−1n⋅n−2n⟶1.

In general,

n(n−1)⋯(n−k+1)nk⟶1.

Therefore:

Proposition

The exponential function has the power series

ex=1+x+x22!+x33!+x44!+⋯.

This is not a separate formula. It is the binomial expansion of the limit definition.

The power series is important because it lets us substitute more than real numbers into the exponential.

3. The Differential Equation y′=ky ​

3.1 The Same Compounding in Time ​

Consider

y′=2y,y(0)=1.

The speed is always twice the current position.

Break the interval [0,1] into n tiny steps of size 1/n.

At time 0, the speed is 2y(0), so after one tiny step:

y(1n)≈y(0)+1n⋅2y(0)=y(0)(1+2n).

After two tiny steps:

y(2n)≈y(0)(1+2n)2.

After n steps:

y(1)=limn→∞y(0)(1+2n)n=y(0)e2.

For general time s, we need ns tiny steps, so

y(s)=limn→∞y(0)(1+2n)ns=y(0)e2s.

Since y(0)=1,

y(s)=e2s.

3.2 General Pattern ​

Proposition

The differential equation

y′=ky,y(0)=c

has solution

y(s)=ceks.

The reason is the same compounding formula:

y(s)=y(0)limn→∞(1+kn)ns=y(0)eks.
kBehavior
k>0exponential growth
k<0exponential decay
k=0constant

Remark

Compound interest and y′=ky are the same phenomenon. In both cases, repeated tiny multiplicative nudges compound into eks.

4. Complex Exponential and Euler's Formula ​

Lecture 17 introduced complex numbers. Now we use the same exponential definition with a complex input:

eiθ=limn→∞(1+iθn)n.

Each factor

1+iθn

is a complex number close to 1 with a tiny imaginary part.

Geometrically:

  • its modulus is approximately 1;
  • its argument is approximately θ/n;
  • multiplying by it is approximately a tiny rotation by θ/n.

Multiplying n such factors gives total rotation

n⋅θn=θ.

So eiθ is the point on the unit circle at angle θ.

Proposition

Euler's formula is

eiθ=cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ.

Special cases:

eiπ=−1,eiπ/2=i,e2πi=1.

4.1 Differential Equation View ​

Let

y(t)=eit.

Then

y′=iy.

Multiplying by i rotates a vector by 90∘. Therefore the velocity is always perpendicular to the position vector.

If velocity is always perpendicular to position, the distance from the origin does not change. Starting from y(0)=1, the motion stays on the unit circle. The speed is constant, so after time θ, the angle swept is θ.

This is the geometric proof of Euler's formula.

4.2 Power Series View ​

Substitute x=iθ into the power series:

eiθ=1+iθ+(iθ)22!+(iθ)33!+(iθ)44!+⋯.

Using

i2=−1,i3=−i,i4=1,

we separate real and imaginary parts:

eiθ=(1−θ22!+θ44!−⋯)+i(θ−θ33!+θ55!−⋯).

These are the Taylor series of cosine and sine, so again

eiθ=cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ.

Attention

The geometric proof explains why the exponential is rotation. The series proof verifies the formula algebraically.

For a general complex number a+bi,

ea+bi=eaebi=ea(cos⁡b+isin⁡b).

The real part a controls growth or decay. The imaginary part b controls rotation.

5. Exponentiating the Derivative Operator ​

Now we substitute an operator into the exponential.

Let

D=ddx.

Define

eD=limn→∞(I+1nD)n.

What does this operator do to a function f(x)?

First understand one small factor:

(I+1nD)f(x)=f(x)+1nf′(x).

5.1 Linear Functions ​

If

f(x)=kx+b,

then

f(x)+1nf′(x)=kx+b+kn=k(x+1n)+b=f(x+1n).

So for a linear function, the operator I+1nD shifts the graph left by 1/n.

5.2 Smooth Functions ​

On a tiny interval, a smooth function is approximately linear. Therefore

f(x)+1nf′(x)≈f(x+1n).

Thus

I+1nD

is approximately the shift-by-1/n operator.

Apply it n times:

f(x)⟼f(x+1n)⟼f(x+2n)⟼⋯⟼f(x+1).

Taking the limit gives:

Proposition

The exponential of the derivative is the shift operator:

eDf(x)=f(x+1).

More generally,

esDf(x)=f(x+s).

5.3 Taylor's Theorem ​

Use the power series for the exponential:

esD=I+sD+s22!D2+s33!D3+⋯.

Apply both sides to f:

esDf(x)=f(x)+sf′(x)+s22!f″(x)+s33!f‴(x)+⋯.

But esDf(x)=f(x+s), so

Proposition

Taylor's theorem is

f(x+s)=f(x)+sf′(x)+s22!f″(x)+s33!f‴(x)+⋯.

The point of view is:

TIP

Taylor expansion is the binomial expansion of the exponential applied to the derivative operator.

6. Matrix Exponential ​

Now replace the number x by a matrix A.

Proposition

The matrix exponential is defined by

eA=limn→∞(I+An)n.

For a system of differential equations

y′=Ay,y(0)=y0,

a tiny time step gives

y(1n)≈y(0)+1nAy(0)=(I+An)y(0).

After ns steps:

y(s)=limn→∞(I+An)nsy(0).

Therefore:

Proposition

The solution of

y′=Ay,y(0)=y0

is

y(s)=eAsy(0).

The remaining question is how to compute eAs.

7. Spectral Formula for eAs ​

Assume A has spectral decomposition

A=λ1P1+λ2P2+⋯+λkPk,

with compatible spectral projections

PiPj=0(i≠j),Pi2=Pi,P1+⋯+Pk=I.

Lecture 15 gave the spectral formula for polynomials:

g(A)=g(λ1)P1+⋯+g(λk)Pk.

For each finite n,

(I+An)ns

is a polynomial in A. Therefore

(I+An)ns=(1+λ1n)nsP1+⋯+(1+λkn)nsPk.

Taking n→∞ gives

(1+λin)ns⟶eλis.

So:

Proposition

If A has spectral projections P1,…,Pk, then

eAs=eλ1sP1+⋯+eλksPk.

This is the payoff of the spectral projection method: to compute an exponential of a matrix, compute exponentials of eigenvalues.

7.1 Concrete Calculation ​

Let

A=(0−123).

Then

det(tI−A)=(t−1)(t−2).

The eigenvalues are 1 and 2. The spectral projections are

P1=A−2I1−2=(21−2−1),

and

P2=A−I2−1=(−1−122).

Therefore

eAs=es(21−2−1)+e2s(−1−122).

For an initial vector

y(0)=(y1(0)y2(0)),

the solution is

y(s)=eAsy(0).

The eigenspace component in Im(P1) grows like es. The eigenspace component in Im(P2) grows like e2s.

The larger eigenvalue dominates as s→∞.

8. Complex Eigenvalues Produce Rotation ​

From Lecture 17, the 90∘ rotation matrix

R=(0−110)

has eigenvalues

i,−i.

The spectral projections are

Pi=R−(−i)Ii−(−i)=R+iI2i=12(1i−i1),

and

P−i=R−iI−2i=12(1−ii1).

They are conjugate to each other, matching the conjugate-pair symmetry from Lecture 17.

Now use the spectral formula:

eRθ=eiθPi+e−iθP−i.

By Euler's formula,

eiθ=cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ,e−iθ=cos⁡θ−isin⁡θ.

Substitution gives

eRθ=(cos⁡θ−sin⁡θsin⁡θcos⁡θ)

Thus the matrix exponential of the 90∘ rotation generator produces rotation by angle θ.

TIP

Real eigenvalues produce growth or decay. Imaginary eigenvalues produce rotation or oscillation.

More generally, if

λ=a+bi,

then

eλs=easeibs.

The real part a gives growth or decay. The imaginary part b gives rotation.

9. Summary ​

One definition has several faces:

eX=limn→∞(I+Xn)n.
XOutputMeaning
x∈Rexcompound growth or decay
iθcos⁡θ+isin⁡θrotation on the unit circle
sddxshift by sTaylor theorem
AseAssolves y′=Ay

The computational bridge is the power series:

eX=I+X+X22!+X33!+⋯.

For matrices, the spectral projection formula makes this computable:

eAs=∑ieλisPi.

The philosophy is:

tiny repeated changes ⟶ exponential transformation.

Exercises ​

  1. Compute

    (1+2n)n

    for n=1,2,10,100 and compare with e2.

  2. Starting from the binomial theorem, derive the first four terms of

    ex=1+x+x22!+x33!+⋯.

  3. Solve

    y′=−3y,y(0)=5.

  4. Use Euler's formula to compute

    eiπ/3,e−iπ/2.

  5. Let D=ddx. Verify directly on f(x)=x3 that

    esDf(x)=f(x+s)

    matches Taylor's theorem.

  6. Let

    A=(0−123).

    Use the projections in §7.1 to compute eA.

  7. For

    R=(0−110),

    verify by direct multiplication that

    ddθeRθ=ReRθ.
